claim: When the same arguments are judged under 'necessarily true' versus 'plausible' wording, valid arguments are accepted at similar high rates, but invalid arguments are accepted far more under the plausible wording. Wording shifts the false-alarm rate most.
agent_test: Run the same item set through the agent with a 'necessarily follows' prompt versus a 'plausibly follows' prompt at equal tokens. Compare hit and false-alarm rates and d'.
audit_note: Heit and Rotello Exp 1 (.89/.22 vs .93/.55, d' 1.68 vs 0.93, via the authors' 2012 chapter) and Lassiter and Goodman 2012 (necessary .82/.41, plausible .94/.82, d' 1.15 vs 0.63; 507 recruited, 485 analysed, 10,185 judgments) verified; slip: Lassiter's valid acceptance differs by 12 points (.82 vs .94), so 'similar' is loose, though the false-alarm shift (.41 vs .82) is far larger.

claim: Wording changes sensitivity (d') in the Heit-Rotello design, not only the cutoff: deduction d' 1.68 vs induction 0.93 (letters, N=40 per cell) and 1.69 vs 0.78 (categories, N=48 per cell). A pure criterion shift predicts equal d'. Numbers verified against the paper text. Whether this proves two processes is disputed (see A01.06-K04, A01.06-K05).
agent_test: Measure d' for the agent under both wordings with confidence ratings or token probabilities so ROC shape can be checked.

claim: The sensitivity gap reappears within one person by changing one modal word (necessary d' 1.15 vs plausible 0.63; 485 analysed of 507 recruited, 10,185 judgments). A one-scale probability model with a word-specific exponent fits it (R2 .32 to .60), so a wording effect on d' does not by itself show two processes. Verified in the full text. Rank order across modal frames: mean Spearman .53, inside the .49 to .64 range that the model plus noise predicts.
agent_test: Same items, two wordings, repeated samples: compare Spearman of answer probabilities across wordings with a noise ceiling from split halves (Lassiter-Goodman got .53 vs a model range of .49 to .64). Use d_a or AUC, not equal-variance d'.

claim: Dissociations (validity matters more under deduction, belief more under induction) are reliably found, yet state-trace analysis needs only one latent dimension in three experiments (N=122, 110, 122) and in a re-analysis of dual-process datasets. One dimension with separate criteria is the best-fitting account so far, not a proven one.
agent_test: Build a state-trace plot for the agent: mean endorsement under the necessary prompt against the plausible prompt across conditions (belief, validity, length, premise count). Check monotonicity.

claim: The one-dimension state-trace result is weak evidence on its own. A null result favours neither side, the human studies tested only causal conditionals, load manipulations had no effect, and a critic (Ashby 2019) says state-trace analysis cannot count systems.
agent_test: None needed; treat the human single-process claim as unsettled when designing the agent.

claim: Only 6 of 16 dual-process datasets cited by Evans and Stanovich (2013) depart reliably from one dimension even with optimistic assumed SDs of .10. With SDs of .20 or .30, none do. Verified in the paper.
agent_test: None; background for how much weight to give dual-process claims.

claim: Belief bias in syllogisms behaves as a criterion shift: believability moves the threshold while discriminability stays constant (constant-discriminability G2 0.23 and 0.001; constant-criterion G2 47.89 and 77.75). Contested on ROC-shape and identifiability grounds.
agent_test: Measure the agent's accept rate for believable vs unbelievable conclusions at fixed validity, with confidence, to split bias from accuracy.

claim: Cognitive capacity and speeding reduce validity sensitivity more than belief sensitivity; low-capacity people lean on belief, most under induction wording. Concurrent load itself had little effect in the state-trace studies.
agent_test: Cut the agent's token budget and track whether validity-check accuracy drops faster than plausibility-judgment accuracy.
audit_note: Findings match Hayes, Stephens, Ngo and Dunn (2018) (capacity x validity chi2 28.30, speeded validity effect .11 vs .25, no speed x belief effect, concurrent load little effect), but three of the listed sources are that same paper and the others (Hayes et al. 2014 review, Trippas fluency study) do not test capacity or speeding on belief, so the claim rests on one study (N=122).

claim: Logic and belief signals run in parallel, and which one interferes with the other depends on problem difficulty. Logic is not always the stronger or faster signal.
agent_test: Compare conflict costs for easy (modus ponens) and hard (three-term syllogism) items at equal tokens, for validity and plausibility questions.

claim: Conditional-inference judgments are well described as a mixture of knowledge-based probability and form-based warrant with one weight. In one small study (N=30) 81% used form information (mean weight .31).
agent_test: Ask the agent for P(conclusion) with and without the instruction to assume the premises; fit a mixing weight per item type.

claim: In LLMs the internal validity and plausibility directions are aligned (cosine 0.48 to 0.64 vs 0.10 to 0.13 for control concepts), alignment predicts content effect (beta .557, p .017), and steering transfers between tasks. This looks like one shared strength signal. Verified in the paper text.
agent_test: Not testable on a closed API model. Test behaviourally: does a plausibility cue flip validity answers as often as a validity cue flips plausibility answers?

claim: Chain of thought cuts the LLM content effect (Qwen2.5-32B 0.348 to 0.096; Qwen3-14B 0.213 to 0.014) without reducing validity-plausibility alignment (Mann-Whitney p=.625). Written reasoning helps even though the entanglement stays. Verified. Counter-evidence: Poddar et al. found zero-shot CoT made no paired difference (McNemar p=.612) on 14 models. Poddar's CoT cue was only 'think step by step' with a one-word answer and no equal-token control, so the conflict is a difference of design, not settled.
agent_test: Compare content effect with and without a written validity check at equal total tokens on matched believable and unbelievable syllogisms.

claim: In Itzhak et al. (2024), instruction-tuned and RLHF models (Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct, GPT-3.5, GPT-4) mostly showed higher belief-bias scores than their pretrained counterparts, and few-shot examples from the same task lowered it noticeably but left substantial bias; Lampinen et al. (2024) found no consistent content-effect difference between instruction-tuned and base PaLM/GPT models, and found that on syllogisms 5-shot examples only slightly weakened the effect while a simple instruction substantially cut bias only on the natural language inference task.
agent_test: Test the agent with and without 2 to 3 same-task worked examples of ignoring plausibility, at equal tokens.
audit_note: Itzhak et al. support that instruction tuning and RLHF mostly raise belief-bias scores and that task few-shot lowers but does not remove it, but Lampinen et al. found instruction-tuned models showed no consistent difference from base models and say a simple instruction substantially cut bias in NLI, so 'a plain instruction is a modest remedy' is unsupported and the instruction-tuning claim is contested.
claim_before_audit: Instruction tuning and RLHF can increase belief bias. Few-shot examples from the same task reduce it but do not remove it, and a plain instruction is a modest remedy.

claim: A two-stage prompt (name the logical form, then check validity on that form) lowers content effect more than a plain deductive prompt, but content effect stays near 50 on the authors' scale.
agent_test: Add an 'abstract the form first' step and measure content effect against a plain validity prompt at equal tokens.

claim: Handing validity to an external solver beats model-only reasoning on most benchmarks (Logic-LM +18.4% over CoT on average; LINC and SatLM agree), but CoT wins or ties where the problem is short, forward-chaining or hard to formalise: PrOntoQA with GPT-4 98.79 vs 83.20, FOLIO with GPT-4 75.3 vs 72.5 (McNemar p=.58). The solver's edge grows with proof depth (ProofWriter gap +7.1 at depth 0 to +39.4 at depth 5) and with premise count (5.3 premises in FOLIO vs 18.8 in ProofWriter). Translation failure is the cost: GPT-4 executable-formula rate 79.9% on FOLIO and 32.6% on AR-LSAT. All results are 2023 models.
agent_test: Route by proof depth and by translation success: shallow or poorly formalisable goes to model reasoning; deep, clean, many-premise goes to solver or code, with CoT fallback when the formula fails and an 'undecided' outcome kept.
audit_note: Logic-LM (18.4% over CoT, PrOntoQA 98.79 vs 83.20, depth gaps 7.1 to 39.4, exe rates 79.9 and 32.6) and LINC (75.3 vs 72.5, p=0.58; 5.3 vs 18.8 premises) verified; 'LINC and SatLM agree' is loose since LINC only ties CoT on FOLIO.

claim: In LLMs, inducing a rule is easier than applying it when induction is executed as code. GPT-4 scored 1.0 on SolverLearner while zero-shot rule application collapsed in counterfactual settings. Elsewhere, models often answer new cases correctly without having the correct rule. Cheng et al. is partly verified (table text garbled).
agent_test: Compare 'state the rule, then apply it' with direct answering on counterfactual-rule items at equal tokens.

claim: Generating hypotheses and checking them by execution beats direct prediction in induction (ARC subset, GPT-4: 17% direct vs 30% summarised hypotheses), and hypothesis generation is the bottleneck (generator 46.4%, implementor 61.2%).
agent_test: Equal-token comparison of single-shot answer vs N hypotheses plus a verification step on a held-out rule-induction set.
audit_note: Wang et al. abstract (17% direct, 30% LLM summaries on 100 ARC problems) and Parab et al. (generator 46.4%, implementor 61.2%) verified; note the generator/implementor figures are from 100 list functions, not ARC, and the Wang abstract does not name GPT-4.

claim: No study found has run an LLM through the Rips/Heit-Rotello design (same arguments, deduction vs induction wording, ROC, d' or state-trace analysis). A second limited search this session (web and arXiv, until the quota ran out) also found none. Nearest work: belief-by-validity interaction under one wording (Lampinen), accuracy gaps (Poddar), task framing with converted items (Abe), and a signal-detection study on factual QA (Cacioli).
agent_test: Run the design on our agent: 2 wordings x validity x believability, with confidence, then state-trace and d'.

claim: GPT-4 matches human property-induction judgments on most classic phenomena but fails premise non-monotonicity (an odd added premise should weaken the argument; the models say stronger). Details: gpt-4-0314; GPT-4 strongly wrong on Specific non-monotonicity items and uncorrelated with humans on single-premise General Mammals arguments; GPT-3.5 matched humans better on General arguments.
agent_test: Probe the agent with premise sets where an odd added premise should lower strength.

claim: Rips (2001) crossover is only a rough crossover. Hayes et al. describe it as close to a single dissociation, and a state-trace re-analysis was consistent with one dimension. Rips (2001) itself was never opened.
agent_test: None.

claim: Premise count hurts LLM validity judgments even on fixed forms: LLaMA-3 8B zero-shot CoT fell from 44.64 to 39.64 to 31.79 as premises went 2, 3, 4 (Pythia 1.4B 18.21, 11.07, 7.86), and only supervised fine-tuning held (99.05, 94.17, 85.36). Separately GPT-4 misreads the effect of an added odd premise on induction strength. Both are open-weight or 2023-model results.
agent_test: Sweep premise count 1 to 5 and add one odd premise to induction items; check that strength falls when it should and that long chains trigger decomposition or a solver.

claim: LLM answers carry a large global yes-bias or no-bias that is separate from discrimination. Raw-likelihood scoring made several models say 'valid' to everything; one 80B model had 99.2% precision and 42.8% recall, another 61.0% precision and 93.1% recall. Rough d' from reported precision, recall and base rate: about 2.55 (strict) vs 1.39 (lenient). Any wording test must measure and remove this bias first.
agent_test: Before testing wordings, run a base-rate-matched validity set and record each wording's accept rate on known-invalid items.
audit_note: Poddar (99.2 precision/42.8 recall for Qwen3-Next 80B Thinking; 61.0/93.1 for Gemma 3 27B; 76 valid of 160) and Lampinen raw-likelihood bias verified; I recomputed d' as 2.56 and 1.39, matching the rough figures (these are derived, not reported).

claim: LLMs show the human belief-by-validity interaction under one 'valid' wording: belief-consistent conclusions are accepted whatever the logic; belief-violating ones are judged with more sensitivity to validity (interaction z>5.9 in PaLM 2-L, Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5). That is a sensitivity-by-condition pattern, so d' can differ by condition inside one wording.
agent_test: Compute d' separately for believable and unbelievable items under each wording.

claim: Sampling temperature is not a clean criterion lever in LLMs. In a pre-registered factual-QA study it changed both criterion and sensitivity (AUC +0.071 to +0.146), and instruct models had unequal-variance evidence (z-ROC slopes 0.52 to 0.63). Plain equal-variance d' is therefore unsafe; use d_a or AUC, and prompt wording as the criterion lever.
agent_test: Fit z-ROC slope from confidence ratings on the agent's own validity judgments before reporting any d'.

claim: Two cutoffs on one strength scale can be moved separately in humans: speeding shifted endorsement in opposite directions for induction and deduction (N=122), and a base-rate experiment moved the two criteria in opposite directions (second-hand through Hayes et al.; Stephens, Dunn & Hayes 2018 not opened). Nothing of this kind has been run on LLMs, so setting the agent's threshold from stated stakes is a design hypothesis only.
agent_test: Tell the agent the stated base rate of valid items (20% vs 80%) or the cost of a false accept, and check that the accept rate on invalid items moves while discrimination stays put.

claim: Models that are strong on form separate the validity question from the believability question; weak ones do not. Syntax accuracy 81.7% vs believability accuracy 56.2% across 14 models; the strongest models had a 47 to 48 point gap and under 2 points of belief bias; the weakest leaned on believability. For strong models a plain validity question is enough; for weak or small sub-models add a form-first step.
agent_test: For each sub-model the agent calls, measure the congruent-minus-incongruent gap once and switch the form-first step on only where the gap is large.

claim: A solver is a strict validity judge: on FOLIO LINC said 'Uncertain' 57% of the time against 41% for CoT, with lower recall and higher precision on True/False, and SatLM can abstain on unsatisfiable or ambiguous formulas. Keeping an 'undecided' outcome in the check route avoids forcing a wrong yes or no.
agent_test: In the check route allow valid, invalid and undecided, and count how often each is returned.
audit_note: LINC (57% vs 41% Uncertain, precision 93% vs 81%, lower recall) and SatLM (abstains on UNSAT/AMBIG) verified; LINC attributes the extra 'Uncertain' mainly to lossy translation to FOL, and the design advice in the last sentence is the researcher's inference, not a source finding.
